draft.title: Radioactive decay and half-life
card: Some atoms have an unstable nucleus. It gives off energy or particles to become more stable. This is radioactive decay.
a particle of two protons and two neutrons. Beta is a fast electron from the nucleus. Gamma is a burst of energy, not a particle.
Alpha is stopped by paper and beta by thin aluminium. Gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.

Half-life is the time for half the atoms in a sample to decay. The decay of one atom cannot be predicted, but a large sample follows a steady pattern. After one half-life, half the unstable atoms are left. After two, a quarter are left.
draft.remember: Unstable nuclei decay by giving off alpha, beta or gamma radiation. Half-life is the time for half the atoms to decay.

a.q: What does the half-life of a radioactive sample tell you?
opts: The time for half its unstable atoms to decay
The time for all its unstable atoms to decay
The time for its radiation to be halved by lead
The time for each atom to lose half its mass
a.why: Half-life is the time for half the unstable atoms in a sample to decay. It does not mean all atoms decay in two half-lives, because only half of the remaining atoms decay in each half-life.
a.clue: Think about how many atoms have decayed, not how long one atom lasts.

b.q: A sample of a radioisotope has a half-life of 6 hours. Mia starts with 80 g of the isotope. How much is left after 12 hours?
b.why: 12 hours is two half-lives. The amount halves from 80 g to 40 g, then from 40 g to 20 g. The tempting answer of 40 g forgets the second half-life.
b.clue: Work out how many half-lives fit into 12 hours.

a.best: The time for half its unstable atoms to decay
